option_scores.rationale: Status quo preserves the existing 12-seat workshop but adds no new capability, no second revenue line, and no ownership asset; it is safe activity without wealth-building motion, so it cannot be endorsed as the answer to the question asked.

A single bounded paid pilot cohort is the only option that converts an unmeasured want into paid evidence while keeping spend inside the hard constraint and leaving the workshop intact; payment in advance is the ownership test, not a survey of interest.

Broad launch now builds fixed delivery load before any paid demand signal exists, and the affordability question inside the critical domain is unresolved; scale applied to an unproven offer multiplies exposure rather than capability.

framework_applications.application: Test the decision against three questions the seat asks of any new activity: does it build a durable capability the practice owns, does it create an asset that outlives the founder's hours, and does it convert effort into wealth rather than into more calendar? The workshop is a delivered service bound to founder time. A group program, if it earns paid commitment, becomes a repeatable product asset with a curriculum, a cohort rhythm, and a waitlist - property rather than labor. The pilot is the smallest test of whether that asset actually forms.

Interest is not demand. The brief records that desire for a group program is unmeasured; the seat's discipline is to make the market speak with money before the practice commits structure. A single pilot cohort priced and collected in advance produces a paid signal that either authorizes the broader build or closes the question cheaply.

decisive_arguments: The question is not whether a group program is a good idea but whether the practice should buy the right to scale it. One pilot cohort buys that right at the lowest possible cost; a broad launch buys it at full cost with no evidence.

Paid enrollment is the only measurement that distinguishes a real asset from more activity. The brief lists wanting a group program as unknown, and no amount of internal enthusiasm resolves an unknown that only the market can settle.
Constraint con-1 forbids displacing the existing workshop. A bounded pilot satisfies this by construction; a broad launch puts the proven 12-seat product at risk against an unproven one.
Enduring wealth in a coaching practice comes from owned repeatable products, not from adding hours. The pilot is a test of whether an owned product can exist, and it fails informatively if it cannot.
strongest_objection: A pilot cohort can become the activity trap it is meant to avoid: a one-off event that consumes founder hours, produces no reusable curriculum asset, and leaves the practice with a new delivery obligation and still no owned product. If the pilot is run as a bespoke favor to known graduates rather than as a priced, repeatable, documented offer, it teaches nothing about scalability and simply adds a second founder-dependent service line. The seat's own standard therefore cuts against a pilot that is not deliberately designed as an asset-formation test with a written curriculum, a fixed price, and a documented delivery cost.

conditions.description: Advance paid commitment must be collected before delivery begins, with a minimum enrollment floor set in advance; enrollment below the floor closes the pilot rather than triggering a discounted extension.
conditions.verification_method: Count completed payments against the pre-declared floor and confirm the floor was fixed before enrollment opened.
required_evidence: Record of completed payments before first session

conditions.description: Pilot delivery must be documented as a reusable asset during the run: written curriculum, session plan, and a recorded per-cohort delivery cost in founder hours.
conditions.verification_method: Inspect the curriculum artifact and the logged founder-hour cost for the cohort before any broader-launch decision.
required_evidence: Founder-hour and direct-cost log for the cohort

conditions.description: Pilot spend must remain inside the invented budget cap and must not reduce workshop capacity or cancel any scheduled workshop cohort.
conditions.verification_method: Compare recorded pilot spend against the cap and confirm the workshop schedule is unchanged for the pilot window.
required_evidence: Pilot spend record against the cap
Workshop schedule before and during the pilot

conditions.description: Financial feasibility of the pilot at committed cash levels must be resolved by the designated critical-domain seat before any pilot spend is committed.
conditions.verification_method: Obtain the designated critical-domain seat's completed feasibility determination and attach it to the decision record.
required_evidence: Completed financial-feasibility determination for the pilot

critical_unknowns: Whether workshop graduates want a group program at all is unmeasured in this invented case, so the demand side of every option is currently an assumption rather than a finding.
Whether the fictional pilot is affordable at committed cash levels is unresolved by the designated critical-domain seat, which caps confidence in the spending case for options B and C.
The founder's available hours for a pilot cohort alongside the existing workshop are not quantified, so the claim that one pilot can be staffed by the founder alone remains an assumption.
change_my_mind: Evidence that a paid pilot cannot be run inside the hard budget cap, or that founder hours are already fully committed by the existing workshop, would move me off B toward A. Conversely, a completed financial-feasibility determination plus pre-collected paid enrollment at or above the declared floor would move me toward endorsing a broader launch, because at that point the asset has been paid for by the market rather than assumed by the practice.
minority_position: Within this seat's own reading, the least comfortable conclusion is that a successful pilot may still be the wrong next step if it produces a founder-dependent cohort model rather than a transferable one; the seat would rather see the pilot structured to expose that failure early than see it judged only on revenue.
